title: An easier gate than Romeo's
text: Hugo invokes Romeo entering Juliet's garden and then deflates it at once: Marius has no wall to scale, only a rusty bar that wobbles 'after the fashion of old people's teeth'. The joke keeps the idyll on the ground. This is a real garden with a broken railing, and the lovers are two very young people, not a legend.

title: Love that ruins or saves
text: 'Love has no middle course; it either ruins or it saves.' Hugo stops to say Cosette, generous and unguarded, 'would have been lost' with a careless lover. A reader who remembers Fantine and Tholomyès hears whose daughter is being spoken of. The mother met the love that ruins. Hugo goes out of his way to tell us the daughter has met the other kind.

title: Euphrasie
text: Cosette confides that her real name is Euphrasie, which Marius has never heard. The reader has known it since Fantine's chapters: Cosette was her mother's pet name for her. She decides she prefers Cosette because he does. In a book full of false and borrowed names, here is a true one shared in the dark, and then gladly set aside for the name that love uses.

title: Full light, at night
text: The chapter is called 'Full Light', yet every scene in it happens after dark, under trees, with the planets turning overhead. For Hugo the light is inward. Two people 'nearer to the archangels than to mankind' make their own daylight in a neglected garden that no one else can see into.

title: Everything except everything
text: 'They had told each other everything except everything.' Marius gives his name, his father's rank and his quarrel with his grandfather. He leaves out the Gorbeau garret, Thénardier and her father's strange flight. The reader holds all the facts the two lovers have not shared, and feels the gap between their innocence and what is known.

title: Blind to the cholera
text: The cholera that the lovers fail to notice was real. It reached Paris in late March 1832 and killed some eighteen thousand Parisians that year, including the prime minister, Casimir Perier. Hugo sets the purest love in his book against the city's worst epidemic. Happiness, he suggests, is also a kind of deafness.

title: No yesterday, no tomorrow
text: Marius 'hardly remembers the morning' by the evening, and neither lover asks where any of this is leading: they 'consider that they have already arrived'. Is this suspension the purest part of their love, or something that leaves them unready for the world? Hugo describes it with delight and gives no verdict.

title: Whitewash on her back
text: Valjean, who has outwitted Javert and climbed convent walls, notices only that Cosette has whitewash on her back. Hugo plays it as gentle comedy: the watchful father defeated by a girl who agrees to everything. The man who has spent his life on guard has stopped thinking that Marius exists.

title: The debt Marius does not see
text: Éponine's 'Good evening, Monsieur Marius' embarrasses him. He owes her his happiness and has not thought of her once. Hugo adds that Marius has not even registered that she is a Thénardier, a name his father's will told him to honour. Notice that she speaks with downcast eyes and leaves abruptly. Marius sees none of it.

title: From light to shadow
text: 'Full Light', 'The Bewilderment of Perfect Happiness', 'The Beginning of Shadow': the chapter titles of this Book follow a day from noon to dusk. Hugo marks the turn not with a disaster but with a greeting on a boulevard that Marius answers awkwardly.

title: The daughter of a wolf
text: Six armed men, her own father among them, are stopped by one starving girl sitting on a kerb. Éponine guards the house of the girl Marius loves against the family she belongs to. When Thénardier pleads that they must eat, she answers 'Burst!' Notice how fully the parent-child relation is reversed: the daughter threatens the father with the police.

title: She no longer talks slang
text: 'It is remarkable that Éponine did not talk slang.' The chapter title promises slang, and the gang speaks it. Hugo has just spent a whole Book on argot as the language of crime and misery. He makes Éponine's dropped slang a sign of what Marius has meant to her: love has changed the very words she uses.

title: The nets at Saint-Cloud
text: Éponine says she does not care whether she is found dead on this pavement tomorrow 'or in the nets at Saint-Cloud' a year hence. Downstream from Paris, nets across the Seine at Saint-Cloud caught what the river carried, including the bodies of the drowned. Her bravado is the bravado of someone who already knows where the city's poor end up.

title: Stopped by omens
text: It is not the law that saves the house in the Rue Plumet. It is a girl's threat and Brujon's superstition: two sparrows fighting that morning, a quarrelsome woman jostled that evening. Hugo gives the underworld its own rules and prophets. These men fear bad luck more than the police.

title: A prose poem in place of a scene
text: This one-paragraph chapter steps out of the street and into a forest. Ruffians become beasts of prey, and the girl at the gate becomes a spectral figure in a shroud. 'The ferocious fear the sinister; wolves recoil when they encounter a ghoul.' Hugo gives the image its own chapter so that it can sink in before the story moves on.

title: The power of having nothing
text: What stops six armed men? Hugo's answer is that Éponine has passed beyond fear: thin, coughing, indifferent to death, she belongs to 'that which emerges from the cemetery'. Poverty has worn her down to something the predators cannot grip. It is a frightening kind of strength, and Hugo does not pretend it is a healthy one.

title: Boots that let in water
text: For six weeks love has floated free of money. One sentence from Cosette brings it down: her father may take her to England. Marius's answer is an inventory of poverty: debts to Courfeyrac, a three-franc hat, boots that let in water, no money for a passport. The pride that made him refuse help now stands like a wall between him and her.

title: An address on the wall
text: Marius scratches '16 Rue de la Verrerie' into the plaster with his penknife, so that Cosette can always find him. Notice the change. For weeks the garden has been a place without writing or witnesses. Now it carries words cut into its wall, and words on a wall can be read by anyone who passes that way.

title: A word of honour
text: Marius gives his word of honour for the first time in his life, 'feeling his father beside him': if she goes, he will die. Then he speaks darkly of a 'he' who receives only in the evening, and Cosette does not understand. Hugo lets a desperate plan form offstage, with Marius himself calling it senseless.

title: What have you come here for?
text: For four years M. Gillenormand has longed for the bell to ring. When it does, joy comes out of his mouth as harshness. Hugo writes two proud men who love each other and cannot say so. Each wants the other to yield first. Notice how the old man summons and dismisses his daughter just to make Marius wait.

title: The word 'Father'
text: Marius, who fought to claim the father his grandfather erased, now calls the old man 'father' in his plea, and that single word undoes him. Gillenormand hauls him into a chair, presses a hundred louis on him and tells him to chatter about his love. Hugo shows how near reconciliation came.

title: Pamela and the lancer's gossip
text: At 'Rue Plumet' the old man recalls Théodule's tale of a 'Pamela' behind a railing, a pretty girl in the eighteenth-century sense of Richardson's heroine. Gillenormand is a man of Louis XV's century, for whom such girls are for amusement, not marriage. 'Make her your mistress' is his idea of generosity. To Marius it is a sword.

title: Father and wife
text: 'Five years ago you insulted my father; today you have insulted my wife.' Marius sets the two insults side by side: the dead father he has made his religion, and a girl he has not married. The old man runs to the window calling his name four times. Hugo leaves him with 'nothing left in his eyes'.

title: The same words, read from the other side
text: The address Marius scratched for Cosette is found by her father, who reads it as a signal to enemies or a warning to himself. The reader knows exactly who wrote it and why. Hugo uses the same twenty letters to show two worlds that never meet: a lover's tenderness and a fugitive's dread.

title: Pépin and Morey
text: Valjean fears that police hunting 'political men like Pépin or Morey' might stumble on him. Pépin, a grocer of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, and Morey, a saddler, were real republican conspirators of the period. Valjean's private danger is now tied to public events. When Paris grows restless, a hidden man is less safe.

title: A message without a face
text: 'Move away from your house.' A folded paper drops from nowhere, and a small figure in a grey blouse and velvet trousers vanishes over a parapet. Valjean's life has been shaped by documents: a yellow passport, a convict's number, borrowed names. Now the warning comes unsigned, and he cannot tell whether it is from a friend or an enemy.

title: Lamarque's funeral sounds like Chinese
text: 'Are you coming to General Lamarque's funeral?' Courfeyrac asks, and to Marius the words mean nothing. Hugo makes history arrive at the moment a young man has lost interest in everything. The revolt his friends have been planning for chapters reaches him only as distant noise from the boulevards.

title: Javert's pistols
text: Marius pockets the two loaded pistols Javert gave him for the Gorbeau ambush, 'without knowing why'. They were handed to him in the service of the police. He now carries them, unthinking, through a city at war with its government. Objects in this book keep passing from one side of the law to the other.

title: A voice through the trees
text: Hugo withholds a face at the climax of the chapter. Marius has decided to die, and the call to the barricade comes as a voice from the dark street, hoarse and half familiar. He sees only someone who looks like a young man running off. The summons that sends him into the revolt comes from someone he cannot see.

title: Why go to the barricade?
text: Marius goes to the Rue de la Chanvrerie because Cosette is gone and dying seems all that remains, not because he believes in the republic. Is that a lesser reason to take up arms, or simply a more honest one? Hugo has given his friends their convictions; he gives Marius only grief.

title: Choosing which child to sacrifice
text: Mabeuf looks over his books 'like a father choosing which child to sacrifice'. Hugo keeps an exact ledger of the decline: twenty sous for a book that cost twenty francs, a Robert Estienne sold to buy an Aldus, an Elzevir sold for the cab fare to a dinner where no one speaks to him. Poverty strips a man who has harmed no one, page by page.

title: Honesty that does not pay
text: Mabeuf handed the purse that fell into his garden to the police as lost property, since he could not believe a star had coined itself into louis. No one claimed it. Hugo gives us one more honest act that changes nothing. Virtue in this book is often its own and only reward.

title: The missing book
text: The chapter ends on a gesture: Mabeuf takes his hat, reaches for a book to put under his arm, finds none and says 'Ah! truly!' His whole life is in that habit. With the last volume sold for Mother Plutarque, he walks out towards the sound of firing, not knowing what else to do with his hands.

title: Giving the other side the floor
text: Hugo opens his history of the rising by letting the opposition speak. The 'golden mean' school says riots shut shops, depress the funds and cost twenty, forty, sixty millions a day. Hugo states their case fairly, even generously, before rejecting it. This digression teaches the reader how to judge what is about to happen in the streets.

title: Effects and causes
text: The bourgeois argument counts effects in francs. Hugo answers that if July 1830 cost a hundred and twenty millions, putting Philip V on the Spanish throne cost two milliards, and he 'would still prefer the 14th of July'. His real question is not what revolt costs but why people rise at all.

title: Two years of riots
text: Hugo writes of the riots that followed 1830 as though everyone remembers them. The July Revolution put Louis-Philippe on the throne but left most people without a vote. The early 1830s brought repeated unrest, including the silk-workers' rising at Lyons in November 1831. June 1832 is one wave in a stormy sea.

title: Insurrection and revolt
text: The chapter gives the book a key word pair. Insurrection is the whole people reclaiming its rights from a usurping fraction. Revolt is a fraction attacking the whole. 'There is no insurrection except in a forward direction.' The same cannon can be wrong one day and right another. Hugo asks us to judge every rising by its direction, not by its violence.

title: The vote as cure
text: Hugo argues that universal suffrage dissolves riots at birth by giving insurrection the ballot. In 1832 the French electorate was tiny: under the July Monarchy fewer than two hundred thousand men could vote, in a nation of over thirty million. Hugo was writing in 1862, after manhood suffrage had arrived in 1848.

title: 'We have seen this'
text: Hugo promises to tell one small, little-known episode of 5 and 6 June, changing a few names. He presents himself as an eyewitness: 'We have seen this.' The novel now claims the authority of testimony. What follows is offered as the foliage of history, the part the historians leave out.

title: General Lamarque
text: Jean Maximilien Lamarque was a real general of the Empire and a liberal deputy, hugely popular with the people. He died of cholera on 1 June 1832. His funeral on 5 June, with Lafayette speaking at the Austerlitz bridge, became the spark of the rising. Hugo follows the historical record closely here.

title: Nobody knows what happened in that minute
text: Dragoons and crowd touch, three shots ring out, and Hugo admits that 'no one knows' who began: a trumpet, a child's dagger-blow? He writes history as a crowd lives it, full of rumour, red flags, a man with a red beard pointed out. The first dead include an officer and an old deaf woman closing her window.

title: A burial and a birth
text: The title calls the funeral 'an occasion to be born again'. Lamarque, who kept the sadness of Waterloo for seventeen years, is carried through Paris with the sword of the Hundred Days. The dead general becomes a rallying point for the living. In Hugo's Paris, funerals are where revolutions begin.

title: Riot as inventory
text: Two hundred and thirty guns, sixty-four swords, eighty-three pistols; twenty-seven barricades in the Halles quarter alone. Hugo's lists turn chaos into a register. The style tells you he is writing history as well as fiction: precise, street by street, as if mapping a battlefield like Waterloo.

title: The author under fire
text: 'The author of this book' sheltered for half an hour behind a half-column in the Passage du Saumon. Hugo really was caught in the fighting of 5 June 1832, and he puts himself in the story as a witness. The novel's narrator steps briefly into the street he is describing.

title: The calm at the centre
text: A third of Paris is in the insurgents' hands. Around the Tuileries 'solitude forms', and Louis-Philippe is 'perfectly serene'. Hugo sets the boiling streets against the stillness of power. The centre of Paris has become a citadel where, he notes, no fighting has yet begun.

title: Billiards beside grapeshot
text: In ordinary riots Paris barely notices: a few streets from the firing, billiard balls click and theatres play vaudeville. In 1831 a fusillade paused to let a wedding pass; in 1839 a cocoa-seller served both sides. Hugo loves this nonchalance as a sign of the city's size and gaiety, the city of Voltaire and Napoleon.

title: This time Paris is afraid
text: Then the tone changes. Shutters close in distant quarters, eight hundred are arrested by nine o'clock, and wives and mothers ask why he has not come home. Hugo brings the rising into private houses. History is now something families wait for behind bolted doors.

title: The tocsin of Saint-Merry
text: Through these chapters one sound recurs: the alarm bell of Saint-Merry, ringing over the city. Hugo builds the night around listening, to cavalry, trumpets and firing, and above all to that 'lamentable' peal. The reader, like the households of Paris, hears the rising before seeing it.

title: Where are my two children?
text: Gavroche still wonders 'where the devil his two children are'. The reader knows they are his own brothers, though he never learned it. He spent a night with his brothers and the dawn with his father without knowing either bond. A child of eleven or so talks like a parent about the only family he chose.

title: A pistol with no trigger
text: Gavroche 'borrows' a holster-pistol from a junk shop and marches off to the wars, only to find it has no trigger. His revolution is courage and theatre without means. Hugo enjoys the joke and lets it stand for something larger: the very poor go to war with whatever they can find.

title: A gamin of letters
text: Who wrote Gavroche's songs? Perhaps Gavroche himself. Hugo makes him a folk poet who mixes the birds' repertory with the workshops'. He once spent three months with a printer and ran an errand for an Academician. The street child is given an authorship of his own, and Paris itself seems to sing through him.

title: Helping the enemy up
text: On his way to fight the government, Gavroche puts down his pistol to help a fallen National Guard lancer, and then the horse. Hugo slips the act in without comment. Gavroche wants to overturn the authorities, but he will not leave a man or a horse lying in the street.

title: Four corners of old age
text: Three portresses and a ragpicker gossip in a doorway, and Hugo notes the hierarchy even here: the ragpicker defers to the portresses, the humble rank of the refuse heap. Their chatter about cats, meat prices and the Duc de Bordeaux is the voice of the Marais, where order is a habit. To them Gavroche is just 'a bastard'.

title: A gaunt poodle
text: Gavroche, insulted as a beggar's brat, pauses to pity a starving poodle 'whose hoops all show'. The street child recognises his own kind. Like his kindness to the lancer's horse, it is a tiny gesture, and it tells us who Gavroche is more surely than his swagger does.

title: A cannonball that is a pebble
text: The barber declares he would rather die of a cannonball in the belly than slowly in bed. A crash, he turns pale, 'a cannonball!', and the old soldier picks up a pebble. Hugo sets the veteran's list of wounds from Marengo to Waterloo beside the barber's bluster, and the comedy deflates both bravado and fear.

title: What has anyone done to that gamin?
text: The hairdresser is outraged: what has anyone done to that gamin? The reader knows. This is the shop where the two little boys were turned out into the rain. Gavroche has not forgotten. His stone is a rough, street-level justice for children nobody else defended.

title: The Emperor's wounds
text: The veteran's catalogue of battles, Marengo, Austerlitz, Jena, Friedland, the Moskowa, Lutzen, Waterloo, runs through Napoleon's whole career. In 1832 such men were still everywhere in Paris, and their memories fed the crowd that buried Lamarque. The Empire is still alive in a barber's chair.

title: Not firing out of the ranks
text: Bahorel tears down the Archbishop's Lenten notice, and Gavroche is won over. Enjolras rebukes him: the Archbishop is not the enemy, and one must not 'fire out of the ranks with the soul' any more than with a gun. Notice how Enjolras wants anger aimed. His revolution has no room for spite.

title: Latin for a gamin
text: 'Hercle!' 'Para bellum!' Gavroche asks what the Latin means and approves once he understands. Hugo enjoys the meeting of the students' classroom culture and the street child's quickness. The band is a mixture of social worlds, and Gavroche picks up their language as fast as he once picked up slang.

title: An old man, unarmed
text: The chapter closes on a figure among the clubs and bayonets: an extremely old man, unarmed, hurrying so as not to be left behind. 'Keksekça?' asks Gavroche. Hugo saves the name for the last line: M. Mabeuf. The book-lover who had nothing left to sell is marching with the insurgents.

title: 'That is good'
text: Fighting, cannon, flinging the government to the earth: to each, Mabeuf answers 'That is good.' The man who once cared only for plants and books now walks with a firm step and 'the face of a man asleep'. Hugo does not give him politics. He gives him the calm of someone who has nothing left to lose.

title: An old regicide
text: The students decide the silent old man must be a former member of the Convention, a regicide. A legend forms around Mabeuf in minutes, because a revolt needs ancestors. Hugo has already shown us one real Conventionist, the dying G. at Digne. This one is only a timid churchwarden whom grief has made fearless.

title: A nonsense ballad as marching song
text: Gavroche marches ahead 'like a trumpet', singing of Charlot and Charlotte and two drunken sparrows, with refrains for Chatou, Passy, Meudon and Pantin. No Marseillaise here. Hugo leads the insurgents towards Saint-Merry to the tune of a street song, the city's own music, cheeky and light.

title: Strangers in the ranks
text: Two newcomers join the band, and Hugo names neither. One is a tall, grey-haired man of bold bearing whom none of the leaders knows. The other is a pale, slight young workman who has waited an hour at Courfeyrac's lodge asking for Marius. A crowd on the march takes in anyone. Hugo lets us see them arrive, and does not explain them.

title: Monsieur de Courfeyrac
text: 'If you call me Monsieur de Courfeyrac again, I shall call you Mother de Veuvain.' Courfeyrac's father really was M. de Courfeyrac, but the republican son has dropped the noble particle. On the way to a barricade he will not be given a title even by his portress. In this book names are always a statement of where one stands.

title: A mob does not go where it intends
text: The band means to reach Saint-Merry, overshoots it and ends up 'without quite knowing how' in the Rue Saint-Denis. Hugo keeps showing chance at work in history. The great events of a rising are placed by wrong turnings, a forgotten hat and a coffer fetched from under dirty linen.

title: A letter for a map
text: As he drew Waterloo as a capital A, Hugo now draws the Halles quarter as an N, with the Rue de la Chanvrerie as one upright. The digression is doing a practical job: it gives the reader a map of a battlefield before the battle. It also says that this tangle of streets is a real place with a three-hundred-year history.

title: A vanished quarter
text: 'All of it vanished' when the Mondétour labyrinth was opened up in 1847, and the Rue Rambuteau 'devoured' the old streets. Hugo, writing in exile in the early 1860s, describes a Paris that no longer existed. Like the convent of the Petit-Picpus, the Corinthe is preserved only in his book.

title: Carpe ho ras
text: Father Hucheloup advertises his stuffed carps, 'Carpes au gras', in his own spelling. Rain washes out two letters and leaves 'Carpe ho ras', so that 'knowing no French, he had equalled Horace'. Hugo loves accidents that turn the ordinary into Latin. The wall of a cheap wine-shop now tells its customers to seize the hour.

title: Out of pity
text: After Hucheloup's death the cooking turns execrable and the wine worse, and the friends keep coming 'out of pity', as Bossuet says. They eat on credit, pay badly and are always welcome. The Corinthe is a picture of loyalty among poor people: the students and the bearded widow keep each other going.

title: A sceptic among believers
text: While Paris boils, Grantaire breakfasts on oysters and harangues: creation is bankrupt, God patches events like a tradesman with an empty till, and the one reality is drink. He is the voice of doubt inside the ABC. Hugo gives him wit and some truth, and lets him drink himself away from the cause his friends serve.

title: Make it here!
text: Bossuet, drunk on a windowsill with his back in the rain, sees the band pass the end of the street and bellows to Courfeyrac: 'This is a good place! Make it here!' That is how the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie is placed. Hugo, who has just lectured on the causes of revolt, shows how its sites are chosen, by chance and by friendship.

title: Sent to Bossuet, not to me
text: Enjolras sends his warning to Bossuet, and Grantaire mutters that Enjolras disdains him. Among all his jokes this is the one remark said without a joke. What does Grantaire want from Enjolras, and why does it matter more to him than the funeral or the riot?

title: A city turned into a wall
text: Iron bars from the wine-shop grating, paving-stones, a lime-dealer's dray, the widow's empty casks, beams from house-fronts, a passing omnibus: in minutes the street is barred higher than a man. Hugo's catalogue shows the barricade as Paris itself, rearranged. Everyday things of the city become a fortification.

title: Non licet omnibus
text: Bossuet hands down 'the ladies', takes the omnibus by the bridle and declares in Latin that not everyone may go to Corinth: 'Non licet omnibus adire Corinthum.' The old proverb, from Horace, meant that not everyone can afford the pleasures of Corinth. Here 'omnibus', 'for everyone', is also the vehicle. Even building a barricade, these students make Latin puns.

title: 'Let me sleep here'
text: Enjolras orders the drunken Grantaire off the barricade, and the rebuke sobers him at once. He looks at Enjolras 'with indescribable gentleness' and asks to sleep there. Enjolras tells him he is incapable of believing, thinking, willing, living and dying. 'You will see,' Grantaire answers, and falls asleep. Grantaire believes in nothing except Enjolras, and Enjolras cannot see it.

title: Jesus with Rothschild's fortune
text: In his drunken dithyramb Grantaire says that if kind hearts had fat purses there would be no more poor, and imagines Jesus Christ with Rothschild's fortune. It is a joke and also the novel's question in the mouth of its scoffer. Goodness without means has been shown again and again: the bishop, Mabeuf, Marius.

title: Consolation, Arab style
text: Courfeyrac 'consoles' Mother Hucheloup by telling her that wrecking her shop avenges a fine she once paid, and Hugo caps it with the tale of an Arab father who evened a slap by slapping his daughter's other cheek. Even as the bullets are cast, Hugo keeps the comedy going. These young men laugh at the edge of danger, and the book laughs with them.

title: Spoons into bullets
text: The establishment's pewter mugs, spoons and forks go into the brazier and come out as bullets; dishcloths become lint for wounds. Notice how the tavern's ordinary life is converted, object by object, into war. Hugo lists the volunteers the same way: a breastplate of grey paper, an awl, a cartridge-box marked 'Public Order'.

title: Brothers without names
text: Pale young men and bronzed longshoremen work side by side, 'brothers who do not know each other's names'. Hugo makes the barricade a fraternity of strangers, built on a shared hope of help at three in the morning, a sure regiment and Paris rising. The word fraternity on the Republic's banner is lived here for an evening.

title: A gun for the children
text: Gavroche goes from man to man demanding a real gun; he had one in 1830, he says. Enjolras answers that when there are enough for the men they will give some to the children. 'Gamin!' 'Greenhorn!' The exchange is comic, but it raises a real question the book has carried since the Thénardier children: what place does a child have in the grown-ups' wars?

title: Correcting the newspapers
text: The papers called the barricade nearly impregnable and as high as a first floor. Hugo corrects them: six or seven feet, with steps inside, a gap at one end, an omnibus pole for a flagstaff. The novelist writes like a military historian checking the record. His precision lets the reader stand inside the redoubt and see its weak points.

title: The coffer opened
text: The square coffer Courfeyrac fetched from under his linen is opened on a table: cartridges. 'A tremor and a silence' pass through the bravest. Up to now the day has been flags, songs and furniture. Thirty cartridges to each man turn the street game into something final.

title: Waiting in the dusk
text: The alarm beating through Paris becomes a noise they no longer hear. They load without haste, Enjolras posts three sentinels, and the twilight thickens among houses 'that seem dead'. Hugo slows the prose to the rhythm of waiting. Darkness is coming in from outside the barricade, and so is something unseen.

title: Love verses with loaded carbines
text: Hugo insists on telling what they did while waiting, 'since it is history': they sat together as in their student days and recited love poems. Prouvaire's poem remembers a garret, a burnt muff, a Dante used as a table for chestnuts. These young men are not only revolutionaries. Their politics come from the same young hearts that wrote poems about love.

title: A poem inside the novel
text: Hugo stops his prose for verses, a whole poem of youth in the Latin Quarter. Its lightness, against 'the funereal calm of the deserted streets', gives it what he calls a pathetic charm. The poem looks back at a love that has passed, while the men around it wait for the attack.

title: A torch for the flag
text: The wax torch is set in a cage of paving-stones so that all its light falls on the red flag and none on the men. Street and barricade sink into gloom; the flag glows, 'its scarlet deepened to a terrible purple'. Hugo stages the barricade like a theatre at night. Only the idea is lit, and the men stay in the dark.

title: Recognition on a child's face
text: Before any word is spoken, Gavroche's face runs through 'every grimace' of disbelief, uncertainty and conviction as he circles the stranger on tiptoe. Hugo stages the unmasking first as mime. Then the questions, and the name: 'Javert.' The tall recruit from the Rue des Billettes has been the hunter all along, and the chapter makes us wait for the word.

title: The mouse who has caught the cat
text: 'It's the mouse who has caught the cat,' says Gavroche. Javert, the law in person, is bound to the post in the middle of a wine-shop by rebels. He does not cry out, and raises his head 'with the intrepid serenity of the man who has never lied'. Hugo grants him dignity even in defeat: he is wrong, perhaps, but he is honest.

title: Judges, not assassins
text: 'Then finish the business with a blow from a knife.' 'Spy, we are judges and not assassins.' Enjolras claims for the barricade the very thing Javert serves: lawful judgement. Each side calls itself the law. Javert is to be shot ten minutes before the barricade falls, and both men speak of it calmly, as a matter of procedure.

title: Prefect Gisquet
text: The card found on Javert bears the signature of 'M. Gisquet', the real Prefect of Police of Paris from 1831 to 1836. Hugo threads real names through his invented ones, as he did with Lamarque and Lafayette. A fictional inspector carries a real man's orders, which makes the fiction feel documented.

title: He killed, therefore I killed him
text: Enjolras executes Le Cabuc for murdering the old porter, then tells the barricade: 'I have judged myself also.' The reader has seen this rigour before, in Javert asking Madeleine to dismiss him for a mistaken denunciation. Hugo sets the revolutionary and the policeman as mirror images. Both are pure, both are merciless, and both apply their law to themselves.

title: Fatality and Fraternity
text: Enjolras calls necessity 'a monster of the old world named Fatality', and says the law of progress is for Fatality to vanish before Fraternity. He uses death but hates it, he says. Hugo calls him 'executioner and priest', and the speech is both a creed and a confession. His friends watch him with admiration mixed with compassion.

title: The porter who said no
text: The old porter at his window cannot even see who is aiming at him. He says 'That cannot be, gentlemen' and is shot under the chin. Hugo ends the image with a head on the sill and a little white smoke. Like the deaf old woman at the Austerlitz bridge, the first innocent dead of the barricade is someone who only wanted to keep his door shut.

title: Le Cabuc and Claquesous
text: Hugo offers, as 'a tradition of the police, strange but probably well founded', that Le Cabuc was Claquesous, the masked member of Patron-Minette who slipped away after the Gorbeau arrests. A police card was found on the body; Hugo says he held the 1832 report in 1848. A man whose life was 'all shadows' ends as a riddle, on the edge of both the underworld and the police.

title: A descent through Paris
text: Marius walks from the Rue de Rivoli, with its gaslight and ices, through shut shops with chatting merchants, then a silent crowd, then the army's bivouacs, into streets 'like a cellar'. Hugo turns the walk into a cross-section of the city, layer by layer, 'like a descent of black steps'. Each stage is darker and quieter than the one before.

title: Two white horses and a shaving dish
text: In the black streets Marius meets the two omnibus horses Bossuet unharnessed that morning, still wandering 'with the patience of brutes'. A stray shot pierces a barber's brass dish, 'still to be seen there in 1848'. Hugo uses small physical leftovers of the day, and his own memory of them, to make the night real.

title: The key to the tomb
text: To Marius the voice through the twilight sounds like destiny: he wished to die, and 'a hand in the darkness offers the key to the tomb'. Notice that he goes to the barricade as a lover in despair, armed by chance with Javert's pistols, not as a convert to his friends' politics.

title: Paris from the air, again
text: 'An owl's view of Paris' answers a famous chapter in Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris (1831), 'A Bird's-Eye View of Paris'. There he rebuilt the medieval city from the towers of the cathedral. Here, from above, the old Halles quarter is a black hole in the centre of Paris, with only Saint-Jacques and Saint-Merry rising out of it.

title: Order means night
text: 'The insurrection's invisible police keep order, that is, night': every window that showed a candle at dusk received a shot. Hugo turns his central image pair upside down. Here darkness is the rebels' protection, and the light belongs to the bayonets tightening in a ring around them.

title: The voice from below
text: Hugo sets the political battle, the schools against the middle classes, inside a deeper sound. In 'wretched old Paris beneath the splendour of happy Paris', the people roar, a voice 'from below like the lion and from on high like the thunder'. Behind the students' principles he wants us to hear the misery the whole book has described.

title: The sword that would not come
text: Marius thinks of his father's sword, sold by his grandfather, and decides it did well not to come: a sword from Marengo would not go to the Rue de la Chanvrerie. Civil war feels like desecrating Colonel Pontmercy. The dead father has become Marius's conscience. Notice that he argues with his father's ghost before he argues with himself.

title: Reason or rationalisation?
text: Marius works his way to a 'splendid rectification': there is only just and unjust war, and the monarchy is itself a foreigner. Hugo remarks on the soul's strange aptitude for cold reasoning in extremity, 'the thread of the syllogism floating unbroken in the storm'. Has Marius found a conviction, or given grief the reasons it wanted?

title: A dead man at the window
text: When Marius looks up, a spectator above the barricade seems 'singularly attentive': it is the porter killed by Le Cabuc, staring, mouth open, blood trailing down the wall. Hugo makes the dead a witness. Marius came here to look death in the face, and this is the first face he sees.

title: The Commander's tread
text: The troops approach with a measured, heavy step, 'like the stone tread of the Commander's statue multiplied into a legion'. Hugo borrows from the Don Juan story, in which the statue of a murdered man walks to dinner and drags the sinner down to hell. The army arrives as something inhuman and inevitable, a law of stone walking through the dark.

title: Two words each
text: 'Who goes there?' 'The French Revolution!' 'Fire!' The whole conflict is reduced to a challenge and an answer. Enjolras does not give his name or his cause; he gives an epoch. Hugo makes the exchange sound like history speaking to itself across a dark street.

title: An unanswered question
text: The volley cuts the flagstaff, and Enjolras asks who will plant the flag again. No one answers; even he feels a thrill. 'Does no one volunteer?' Hugo ends the chapter on that silence, and the title, 'Act First', tells us the barricade is being staged as a drama with a second act to come.

title: A churchwarden becomes '93
text: The insurgents cry 'It is the member of the Convention!' as Mabeuf climbs, and in the torchlight they think they see 'the spectre of '93'. Courfeyrac knows better: a 'brave blockhead', a gentle botanist. Enjolras answers: 'The head of a blockhead and the heart of a Brutus.' The barricade needs a legend, and it makes one out of a timid old man.

title: 'This is our flag now'
text: Enjolras kisses the dead man's brow, lifts off his coat and holds up its bloody holes: 'This is our flag now.' The red cloth has fallen and a man's body takes its place. He tells his friends to defend this dead old man as they would a living father. The barricade has found its symbol in a person.

title: Why does Mabeuf climb?
text: Hugo describes Mabeuf's eyes as lit 'with the mournful flame of aberration'. He sat for hours with his head thrust forward 'as if gazing over a precipice', and he cries 'Death!' along with 'Republic!'. Did he die for the Republic, or of the slow loss of everything he loved? Is it possible to separate the two?

title: A title that warns
text: 'Gavroche Would Have Done Better to Accept Enjolras' Carbine.' Hugo announces the mistake before we see it, then delivers it inside the chapter: the giant guardsman, the trigger, nothing. The title turns the scene into suspense. We know the gun will fail; we do not know what will happen to the boy when it does.

title: Javert's weapons
text: Gavroche's borrowed gun, taken from Javert, is not loaded. The shots that save him come from Javert's two pistols in Marius's hands. The policeman's weapons, scattered by chance, fail and save on the rebels' side. Meanwhile Enjolras tells the bound Javert, as Mabeuf's body passes: 'It will be your turn presently!'

title: Bahorel falls
text: Bahorel, the scarlet-waistcoated joker who loved a riot 'like a fish in water', kills the first guard over the barricade and is killed by the second. Hugo gives his death one line, in the middle of the scramble. On a barricade death does not wait for a speech, and the tone of the book changes with it.

title: What one misses in battle
text: As a soldier aims at Marius, a hand is laid over the muzzle; the young workman in velvet trousers falls. Marius 'barely registers' the gun, the hand or the shot. Hugo notes that 'in such moments everything vacillates and one pauses for nothing'. The narration shows us something that its hero does not see.

title: The power of a man who wants to die
text: Marius stands with a torch over a broken powder barrel: 'Blow up the barricade, and yourself with it!' 'And myself also.' The troops flee. Like Éponine at the Rue Plumet gate, he wins because he no longer fears death. Hugo calls him 'the young revolution after the apparition of the old', following Mabeuf onto the stones.

title: Close enough to talk
text: After the first volley, the leaders stand unsheltered with their backs to the houses, facing soldiers 'so close they could talk without raising their voices'. 'Lay down your arms!' 'Fire!' Hugo strips the fight to a few yards of street and a cloud of smoke. When it clears, both sides reload in silence.

title: 'You are he!'
text: Marius asks who the chief is, and Enjolras answers: 'You are he!' Two months ago he was a lover in a garden; now he leads an insurrection. Hugo calls it a nightmare he must make an effort to believe real. History has picked up a young man who came only to die and has made him a leader.

title: Your friends have just shot you
text: Combeferre proposes exchanging Javert for the captured Prouvaire. Then a voice at the end of the street cries 'Long live France! Long live the future!', a shot, silence. Enjolras turns to Javert: 'Your friends have just shot you.' Each side now holds the other's justice in its hands, and the logic of exchange becomes the logic of reprisal.

title: The end of the verses
text: The chapter title calls Prouvaire's death 'the end of the verses'. A few hours ago the gentle poet was murmuring love poems in the dusk. His last lines are a shout for France and the future. Notice that Hugo lets us hear only his voice; we never see him die.

title: Not even seen
text: In his daze Marius does not recognise Javert, bound to his post, and in fact 'has not even seen him'. Javert has watched the whole assault 'with the resignation of a martyr and the majesty of a judge'. Hugo keeps the two men in one room without letting them meet, and the reader is the only one who sees them both.

title: To die together
text: Éponine led Marius to the barricade so that they would die together, and then put her hand over the gun aimed at him because she wanted to die first. Both things are true at once. Hugo does not tidy her love into pure sacrifice or pure jealousy. 'You thought me ugly, didn't you?' is the question of a girl who has never been looked at.

title: A girl in men's clothes
text: The young workman in velvet trousers was Éponine. The disguise makes literal what Marius has always done: looked at her without seeing her. She has been beside him in the garret, at the gate, in the street, and he has never quite known who was there. Only now, with her head on his knees, does he say her name.

title: 'My brother is here'
text: Hearing Gavroche sing, she whispers: 'My brother is here. He must not see me. He would scold me.' Marius has just been thinking bitterly of the duty to the Thénardiers that his father left him. Now he learns the singing boy is Thénardier's son. The debt in the colonel's note has turned into a child on this barricade.

title: The things she remembers
text: Dying, Éponine recalls looking into his mirror, the day by the washerwomen when the birds sang, the hundred-sou piece she refused and hopes he picked up. He had forgotten all of it. Notice how much of her love is made of these small scraps of his attention. 'I believe that I was a little bit in love with you.'

title: The agony of life
text: The title sets two agonies side by side: the agony of death after 'the agony of life'. 'Oh! How happy I am! Everyone is going to die.' For Éponine, who has known hunger, cold and her father's crimes, death beside Marius is the first moment that is hers. Hugo lets the line be terrible and tender together.

title: The pieces assemble
text: Now Hugo explains: Éponine threw the warning on the Champ-de-Mars, was the 'young workman' Cosette gave her letter to, waited at Courfeyrac's lodge, and was the voice at the gate. Scenes the reader saw from outside fall into place. Hugo keeps the explanation short; he has trusted us to carry the separate moments until now.

title: He did not know her handwriting
text: 'Such was the innocence of their love that Marius did not even know her handwriting.' Two months of nights in the garden, and not one letter. The first words Cosette ever writes to him reach him through the hands of the girl who kept them back, and he reads them by a wine-shop candle on a barricade.

title: Carry my body to my grandfather
text: Marius writes in his pocketbook: 'My name is Marius Pontmercy. Carry my body to my grandfather.' The young man who walked out of the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire twice, insulted, still names the old man as his home. And he sends Gavroche away with the letter partly to save him: Thénardier's son is the one debt of his father's he can still pay.

title: A profound calculator of distances
text: Marius says the barricade will not be attacked before daybreak; Gavroche hesitates, snatches the letter and runs. His private plan: it is barely midnight, the Rue de l'Homme Armé is close, he can deliver it now and be back in time. Hugo's ironic title praises a child's arithmetic. Gavroche wants to keep both his errand and his place in the fight.

title: A mirror that rights the letters
text: Cosette's blotting-book lies open by the sideboard, and the slanting mirror rights the reversed imprint of her note. Valjean reads it twice and does not believe it, then understands. Chance brings the truth to him backwards, by reflection. 'The light of the world is eclipsed.'

title: Every kind of love at once
text: Hugo says Valjean loves Cosette as a father, but a father made of grandfather, son, brother and husband, 'with even a mother included'. A lonely man has put every love he never had into one. That is why the discovery is the most terrible of his trials. Another person is the goal of her heart, and he is only her father.

title: The spectre called Hate
text: The man who 'laboured so long to turn all misery into love' looks into himself and sees Hate. Hugo has shown Valjean's conscience at war before, in the long night of 'A Tempest in a Skull'. This time the enemy is not fear of the galleys but jealousy, and he has fallen to the bottom of the precipice 'without perceiving it'.

title: Three men on three posts
text: Valjean goes out bareheaded and sits on the stone post at his door. Mabeuf sat on his overturned post in the rain; Marius sat on a post at the edge of the barricade and thought of his father. Hugo keeps placing his people on these little stone markers at the moment of decision, motionless while Paris fights around them.

title: A coin for a child
text: Valjean lays a five-franc piece in a hungry boy's hand. The reader remembers another coin, forty sous, that Valjean once put his foot on and stole from little Petit-Gervais. Gavroche refuses the bribe, then takes it 'for his mother'. Neither knows that the mother is Madame Thénardier, the woman who worked the child Cosette like a servant.

title: An enemy of light
text: Gavroche smashes the lantern opposite No. 7 because 'they still have their lanterns here, which is disorderly'. Behind the curtains people cry that '93 has come again. In this night darkness serves the barricades. Hugo adds that while the tocsin rings and Saint-Paul strikes eleven, 'the tocsin is man and the hour is God'.

title: 'I am the person'
text: Valjean, who gave himself up in court rather than let another man bear his name, claims to be the person the letter is for. 'You? You are not a woman.' It is a small lie, told on impulse, and it puts a letter meant for Cosette into his hands. Hugo does not comment. He lets us watch it happen.

title: A frightful joy
text: 'I die. When thou readest this, my soul will be near thee.' Valjean seizes on those two lines and feels 'a frightful cry of inward joy'. He need only keep the note in his pocket. Hugo does not hide or soften the feeling. Opening the paper 'smacks of theft', and the hero is shown wishing a young man dead.

title: The missing debate
text: In 'A Tempest in a Skull' Hugo gave a whole night to Valjean's struggle. Here he writes: 'Having said all this to himself, he becomes gloomy. Then he goes downstairs and wakes the porter.' The struggle happens off the page, and we see only what he does next. The reader is left to guess what passed between the joy and the uniform.

title: In the uniform of order
text: An hour later Valjean goes out in the full costume of a National Guard, with a loaded gun and a box of cartridges, towards the markets. The former convict wears the uniform of the citizens who keep order. In this book clothes keep changing a man's place in the world: a yellow coat, a mayor's sash, a gardener's knee-bell, now this.

title: Where is he going?
text: Valjean has the letter, the joy, and a uniform. He has said nothing to Cosette and nothing to us. What does he mean to do at the markets, and which part of him has decided it? Hugo has given us all his reasons for wishing Marius dead and none for what he does next.

title: Received thy cart
text: Gavroche tips a drunken Auvergnat out of his handcart and leaves a receipt: 'French Republic. Received thy cart. Gavroche.' The insurgents have been chalking receipts on doors for requisitioned guns all day. The street boy copies the forms of revolution exactly, and makes them comic by doing so.

title: How history records a prank
text: A boy with a cart and a song sets off a quarter-hour of blind musketry that 'kills several panes of glass'. The Auvergnat is later hauled before the councils of war as an accomplice, and the Marais remembers 'The nocturnal attack by the post of the Royal Printing Establishment'. Hugo shows the comic side of official history.

title: Où vont les belles filles
text: Gavroche sings his way through the empty Marais, listing girls' names, Atala, Agnès, Paméla, Stella, with grimaces nobody sees in the dark. His song runs right through the chapter and picks up new verses after the fusillade. In a city of shut shutters, a child's voice is the only cheerful thing on the streets.

title: A digression that leaps sixteen years
text: Volume V opens in June 1848, outside the story's time. Hugo describes two giant barricades so that we can measure the small one of 1832 against them. The digression gives scale: the Rue de la Chanvrerie is one cell in a long history of Paris rising. It also warns us not to read the next chapters as a simple fable of good rebels and bad soldiers.

title: Hugo in June 1848
text: In the June Days of 1848 the Paris workers rose against the new Republic after it closed the National Workshops, and the army crushed them. Hugo, then an elected representative, stood on the side of order. Here he speaks of 'the rabble' with 'pain and respect': the honest man must resist the suffering crowd 'with a sad conscience'. It is a confession as much as a history.

title: The dragon and the sphinx
text: The Saint-Antoine barricade is a three-storey heap of houses, rags and noise, 'a heap of filth and a Sinai'. The Temple barricade is a straight, silent wall where every passer-by falls to an unseen marksman. Hugo sets fury against cold method, and gives them two builders: a stormy naval officer and a pale former galley-slave who had killed a policeman at seventeen.

title: A cross in the candlelight
text: In the taproom, the 'hall of the dead', Javert stands bound upright to his post and Mabeuf lies under his black cloth. Hugo notes that the prisoner and the corpse 'made a kind of cross'. Law and the old man's despair are laid across each other in one image, lit by candles, in the middle of a wine-shop.

title: Words cut into walls
text: Feuilly, the orphan fan-painter, spends his rest carving 'Long live the peoples!' on the wall with a nail. Courfeyrac chalked a joke on the Corinthe door; Marius scratched his address into a garden wall. Writing on walls runs through these chapters: messages left by people who may not be there to say them.

title: Remorse in a liberating killing
text: At dawn Combeferre talks of the dead, Prouvaire, Bahorel, Mabeuf, even Le Cabuc, and says that even a killing that frees leaves more remorse than joy. Then he drifts to the Georgics, Caesar and Brutus. Hugo's title asks what one does in the abyss if one does not converse. These students face death the way they faced exams, by talking.

title: 'You are abandoned'
text: The barricade expects a regiment to come over at six and Paris to rise at noon. Enjolras returns from scouting and tells the truth: a third of the army is coming, the people are not stirring, 'You are abandoned.' Hugo gives the leader the courage of plain speech. The chapter title, 'Light and Shadow', is the passage from hope to that sentence.

title: The anonymous hero
text: A voice from the darkest part of the crowd answers: raise the barricade, stay, offer 'the protest of corpses'. No one ever knew who spoke. Hugo honours a man in a blouse who says the decisive word and vanishes. In a book where names are hidden and changed, the bravest sentence on the barricade belongs to no one.

title: Mothers at the windows
text: Combeferre's appeal is about those left behind: mothers watching at candlelit windows, daughters who, left without bread, 'would be driven to the street and the police', a child dead in the Necker Hospital with ashes in his teeth. The reader has seen that road to the street in Fantine's story. 'To die was fine; to make others die was murder.'

title: Minus five, plus one
text: Five men are chosen to live, and there are only four uniforms. Then a fifth uniform falls on the pile. Hugo makes Valjean's entrance an act of arithmetic and of giving: before he says a word, he has saved a stranger. 'Who is he?' 'A man who saves others.' Marius, astonished, says only: 'I know him.'

title: Why has he come?
text: Hours ago Valjean felt 'a frightful cry of inward joy' at the thought of Marius's death. Now he is inside the barricade, silent, helping the fifth man into his uniform. Hugo gives no reason. What has happened between the letter and this moment, and what does Valjean mean to do here?

title: Forgetting his own mother
text: Hugo adds a quiet sting to Combeferre's speech: Combeferre, who was not an orphan, 'remembered other men's mothers and forgot his own'. The noble appeal is also blind. Hugo admires his idealists and still notices what they leave out.

title: The twentieth century will be happy
text: Enjolras imagines cities flooded with light, nations as sisters, free and compulsory schooling, 'the right to the alphabet', and no more famine, prostitution or scaffold. 'The nineteenth century is great, but the twentieth will be happy.' The speech is Hugo's own creed of progress, given to a young man who expects to die before morning.

title: Saint-Just and Cloots
text: Hugo says Enjolras had 'too much of Saint-Just and not enough of Anacharsis Cloots'. Saint-Just was the young, austere theorist of the Terror; Cloots, a Prussian baron turned revolutionary, called himself the 'orator of the human race'. Enjolras has the pure, severe republic in him. Combeferre has been teaching him a gentler, worldwide one.

title: A tomb flooded with dawn
text: 'Here misery met the ideal, the day embraced the night.' The barricade, Enjolras says, is made of two heaps, of ideas and of woes, and whoever dies on it enters 'a tomb all flooded with dawn'. Hugo's long contest of light and darkness becomes the whole argument of the speech. There is no applause, only a whisper like leaves.

title: Hearing the prophecy now
text: Hugo wrote Enjolras's speech in the 1860s, and France made primary schooling free and compulsory in the 1880s. A reader today knows what the twentieth century brought. How should we hear 'the twentieth will be happy'? As naive, as a promise betrayed, or as a hope worth holding all the same?

title: 'It is perfectly simple'
text: Bound on the table, Javert notices a shadow, looks up and recognises Jean Valjean. He does not start. He lowers his eyelids proudly and says: 'It is perfectly simple.' After hundreds of pages of pursuit, Hugo makes the recognition almost silent. To Javert the world is still in order: the convict is here among the criminals, where he belongs.

title: A glass of water
text: Enjolras, who has sentenced Javert to death, holds a glass of water to his lips himself, and moves him from the post to the table at his request. Mercy and execution sit side by side in the same man. Javert asks for no favour except to lie down 'like that other man', the dead Mabeuf.

title: Everyone comes here to die
text: Marius does not ask why M. Fauchelevent is here. In his despair 'it seemed natural that the whole world should come there to die'. Fauchelevent does not look at him, which suits Marius, who has always found that man impossible to address. Grief has made Marius incurious, and Hugo shows how close that is to blindness.

title: A fortress and a rat hole
text: At dawn the Mondétour lane is walled up, and the redoubt has three fronts and no exit: 'a fortress but a rat hole too,' laughs Courfeyrac. Each man picks his place 'as at the theatre', and Hugo notes that peril produces order. The only sound when Enjolras takes his post is the cocking of guns.

title: Christ over Napoleon
text: Combeferre lectures on the brass eight-pounder and ends with a sum: a cannonball travels six hundred leagues an hour, light seventy thousand a second, 'the superiority of Christ over Napoleon'. Even under artillery fire these young men argue in images of light. Hugo lets the joke carry his conviction: ideas outrun force.

title: Present!
text: The cannonball and Gavroche arrive at the same instant, and the boy makes 'a greater sensation than the cannonball'. The barricade bursts out laughing. Hugo times the return like stage comedy. The first shot of the artillery is upstaged by a child shouting 'Present!' as if at school roll-call.

title: He might be your brother
text: Combeferre begs Enjolras to look at the young blond sergeant: he has a family, he is probably in love, 'he might be your brother'. 'He is.' 'He is mine too, let us not kill him.' 'Let me alone. It must be done.' A tear runs down Enjolras's marble cheek as he fires. Civil war, as Marius thought on the edge of the barricade, is war between brothers.

title: A letter in the wrong hands
text: Gavroche lies that he gave the letter to the porter. Marius wonders whether the letter and M. Fauchelevent's arrival are connected, then decides perhaps Fauchelevent is simply a republican. The reader knows exactly where the letter went. Hugo lets us watch Marius come close to the truth and turn away from it.

title: The grapeshot
text: Infantry builds a low wall behind the gun; the muzzle shifts slightly left; grapeshot hits the cut and rebounds, leaving two dead and three wounded. Hugo follows the artillery's method with a soldier's eye. The battle is now a technical problem, and the barricade is losing it.

title: The marksmanship that condemned him
text: The long title recalls 1796, when Valjean's skill as a poacher counted against him at his trial for stealing bread. Now that same 'infallible marksmanship' cuts two ropes against the sky and brings down a mattress. The talent the law once used against him becomes the thing that saves a barricade full of strangers.

title: Glory to the thing that yields
text: The old woman's mattress, hung at her attic window back when the barricade was built, now stops the grapeshot. Bossuet laughs at the 'immorality' of a mattress that annuls a cannon: 'glory to the thing that yields'. It is a joke that fits the book. Softness and endurance defeat force more often than force defeats them.

title: 'Citizen, the Republic thanks you'
text: Valjean walks out through the bullets, carries the mattress back on his shoulders and fixes it in the breach. 'Citizen, the Republic thanks you.' The escaped convict is honoured by the barricade's young lawgiver without being known. Notice that he protects the barricade without killing anyone.

title: Carriage gates in the distance
text: Cosette wakes smiling, sure Marius has her letter and will come today. She hears sharp shocks far off and thinks people are opening and shutting carriage gates early. It is the cannon. Hugo cuts from grapeshot to a girl's bedroom and lets the reader hear what she cannot.

title: A martins' nest
text: Below her window a mother martin spreads over her brood while the father flies to and fro with food. Cosette gazes at 'that small family' with a trouble she cannot name. Hugo sets a complete, ordinary family in the cornice of a house in a city full of broken ones. It is the life she wants and cannot yet picture.

title: A chamber not described
text: Hugo refuses to describe a young girl rising: 'one may show a nuptial chamber but not a virginal one.' He keeps the camera outside her door. The tact matters, because Cosette is all expectation. She looks at the sky instead of the walled court, 'as if he might come from there'.

title: Missing nothing, killing no one
text: A fireman and then an officer look down into the barricade from a roof. Valjean knocks each one's helmet off with a single bullet, and no one appears there again. The title states the paradox. He is the best shot on the barricade and he will not kill. When Bossuet asks why, 'Jean Valjean made no reply.'

title: The silence of the barricade
text: Hugo explains the besiegers' tactic: fire for hours so the insurgents waste powder, then assault when their fire slackens. Enjolras does not fall for it, and the barricade stays silent. Meanwhile Gavroche puffs his cheek at each volley and tells the soldiers to rip up more cloth if they want lint.

title: Disorder on the side of order
text: The title is a paradox, and Hugo means it. The suburban National Guard fought for order with no order at all: captains attacked on inspiration, and platoons set themselves up as courts and shot a prisoner in five minutes. That is how Jean Prouvaire died. The law's defenders could be as lawless as the barricade.

title: Killed by order
text: Captain Fannicot, furious at Mabeuf's coat, which he takes for a black flag, throws his company at the barricade without orders. He loses fifteen men and then dies under his own side's cannon, which 'had received no order to stop'. Hugo's dry phrase, 'killed by order', carries the whole irony of the scene.

title: One against a hundred
text: Enjolras is angry at the wasted shots, and Hugo calls him 'the true general of insurrection'. A rising has a fixed number of men and cartridges; repression has the army and the arsenal of Vincennes. The barricade always loses, Hugo says, unless revolution itself rises and the army, 'that lion', finds France, 'that prophet', standing in its way.

title: Good by gunshots
text: 'He has not answered my question,' Bossuet mutters, and Combeferre replies that the silent marksman is 'a man who does good by gunshots'. The insurgents have no name for Valjean except what they see him do. To them he is a puzzle, a crack shot who aims at helmets.

title: Lightning without thunder
text: For an hour on the morning of the 6th Paris seems to wake: barricades begun, a young man killing a cavalry officer, crockery raining from roofs. Then it is gone, 'a flash of lightning without thunder'. Hugo lets hope cross the barricade like weather, and then lets it pass.

title: Old women and chamber-pots
text: When crockery rains on the troops from the roofs of the Rue Planche-Mibray, Marshal Soult remembers what Marshal Suchet said at the siege of Saragossa in 1809: beware of old women and their chamber-pots. Saragossa held out house by house against Napoleon's army. Hugo's real incidents of the 6th of June show the city resisting in small, scattered ways.

title: Die without anything to eat?
text: An insurgent asks whether they are really going to die like this, without eating. Enjolras nods without taking his eyes off the street. Hunger has been the book's subject since Valjean's loaf of bread. Now it is simply one more fact of the barricade, accepted in silence.

title: Patria
text: Bossuet theorises that all heroism comes from women, and that a man without a woman is 'a pistol without a trigger', like Gavroche's pistol. How can Enjolras, with no mistress, be so cold and so bold? Enjolras seems not to listen, then murmurs: 'Patria.' The title promised his mistress's name, and this is it.

title: Jokes in place of wine
text: With no food and the brandy rationed, Courfeyrac and Bossuet 'poured out gaiety in place of wine'. The cannon's grapeshot is 'only a cough'; Courfeyrac announces a second gun like an usher: 'My name is Eight-Pounder.' Hugo keeps the friends' wit alive to the end. It is a form of courage, and of friendship.

title: Success that ruins
text: The barricade's volleys cut down two-thirds of the gunners. 'Success,' says Bossuet. Enjolras shakes his head: another quarter-hour of such success and there will be no cartridges left. The last line is very short: 'Gavroche, it appears, overheard him.' Hugo ends the chapter there.

title: The fault of Voltaire
text: Gavroche's song, 'it's the fault of Voltaire... the fault of Rousseau', mocks a familiar line of the Restoration, when the Church and the royalists blamed the philosophers of the Enlightenment for the Revolution and every evil since. The street child turns their complaint into a joke and throws it back at the soldiers with every bullet.

title: Joy his character, misery his trousseau
text: 'Joy was his character and misery his trousseau.' Hugo began Volume III by describing the gamin of Paris as a species, a pearl in the mud. Here the type becomes one boy, singing in the street, collecting cartridges among the dead, 'the invulnerable dwarf of the fray'. The soldiers laugh as they aim.

title: An unfinished line
text: Hit once, Gavroche sits up, blood on his face, and sings again: '...the fault of...' He did not finish. A second bullet stops him. Hugo breaks the song off in the middle of a word, so that the line is never completed. 'That grand little soul had taken its flight.'

title: The little bird
text: 'He was not a notary, he was a little bird.' From the first pages about the gamin, Hugo has likened him to the sparrow of the streets. He sings like a bird, hops between bodies like one, and in the last sentence his soul takes flight. The image runs through the whole portrait of the street child.

title: From a brother to a father
text: Gavroche once took the two lost boys in, fed them and gave them a bed in the elephant. Now, alone in the Luxembourg, the elder fishes a wet brioche out of the swans' basin and keeps the small half, giving the large one to his brother. The title names what has happened. A child has become a parent, as Gavroche did, without knowing anyone taught him.

title: A lesson in compassion for animals
text: A comfortable bourgeois, possibly the one Marius once heard counselling his son against excess, throws his son's stale brioche to the swans 'to teach compassion for animals', while two ragged children watch from behind the hutch. He calls the firing 'the Saturnalia' and the boys 'anarchy'. Hugo's satire is quiet and exact.

title: Thinkers who forget to love
text: Hugo pauses on 'magnificent egoists' like Horace and Goethe, so filled with the zodiac that they do not see the weeping child. They are great and pitiable at once. The garden is all flowers, bees and breakfasting birds, 'not a beast's stomach empty', and two hungry children walk through it unseen.

title: The garden at eleven
text: Hugo turns from the barricade to the Luxembourg, closed by police order and empty, at the same hour. The cut is abrupt and deliberate. Events of world importance are happening a mile away, and here the drama is a cake in a pond.

title: The dead father waits
text: The Latin title means 'The dead father awaits the son who is about to die'. It gathers up Marius's thought on the edge of the barricade, when he argued with Colonel Pontmercy's ghost. At the chapter's end, among the jokes and the cartridge-making, Marius is 'troubled about what his father was going to say to him'.

title: What Thénardier did for my father
text: Marius carries Gavroche's body back, thinking that what Thénardier did for his father he is now doing for Thénardier's son. But Thénardier brought the colonel back alive, and Marius brings the child back dead. The reader knows that the 'rescue' at Waterloo was a robbery. The son repays a debt that was never owed.

title: One shawl for two
text: They lay Gavroche on Mabeuf's table and spread the widow's black shawl over both: 'there was enough of it for the old man and the child.' The eighty-year-old who sold his last book and the boy who had nothing to sell lie under one cloth. Hugo needs only one sentence for it.

title: Defending without fighting
text: Valjean shakes his head at his share of cartridges. Combeferre calls him an eccentric who has found a way of not fighting in a barricade; Enjolras answers that this does not stop him defending it. Hugo lets the insurgents describe, without understanding it, a new kind of courage.

title: 'That is just'
text: Valjean asks, as his reward, to be the one who shoots the spy. Javert raises his head, sees who it is, and says: 'That is just.' In Javert's world this is the natural order: the convict kills the policeman when he can. He expects nothing else, and in his eyes the request only confirms what Valjean is.

title: Death as a masterpiece
text: Enjolras walls the windows, plans the loopholes, nails up the kitchen door so the wounded will not be splashed, and counts twenty-six men and thirty-four guns. Hugo says he felt that since such men were to die, 'their death should be a masterpiece'. Asked who will drink the fifteen bottles, he answers: 'They.'

title: Blood under the nails
text: Hugo opens with a remark about memory: one comes out of civil war as out of a dream, with blood under one's nails and no clear recollection. The barricade is calm inside and still a vision to those in it. He is telling us how unreliable the survivors' accounts of such days are.

title: Revenge as freedom
text: The title promises revenge, and Javert asks for it: 'Take your revenge.' Valjean takes out a knife and cuts the cords. 'You are free.' The reader remembers the bishop handing a thief his candlesticks. Valjean now does to his pursuer what was once done to him, and repays a lifetime of hounding with release.

title: Giving his enemy the address
text: Valjean adds that if he leaves alive, he lives as Fauchelevent at No. 7, Rue de l'Homme Armé. He hands the policeman his name and his door. Javert repeats the number, snarls 'Have a care', and walks off. A man who has spent years hiding chooses, here, to hide nothing.

title: The lost 'thou'
text: 'You annoy me. Kill me, rather,' Javert shouts, 'not noticing that he had stopped addressing Valjean as thou.' In French the familiar 'tu' is used to inferiors and convicts. Javert's grammar shifts before his mind does. Something in his view of Valjean has moved, and he has not noticed it himself.

title: Two shots, two meanings
text: Valjean fires the pistol into the air and returns: 'It is done.' At that moment Marius has just learned the prisoner's name and recognised the inspector of the Rue de Pontoise. To him the shot means an execution. The reader knows it was a release. The same sound tells the truth to us and a lie to Marius.

title: A pause before the end
text: Just before the final assault, Hugo stops the battle to judge it. The title gives his verdict: the dead are in the right and the living are not in the wrong. He defends the insurgents and the people who would not open their doors. The digression asks the reader to hold both sympathies at once.

title: Every blade has two edges
text: 'An insurrection is an idea sitting its examination before the people.' Utopia that takes up arms almost always comes too soon. And it borrows battle 'from the lie of yesterday': it shoots spies and executes traitors. Hugo, who has just shown Le Cabuc's execution and Javert's sentence, does not exempt his heroes.

title: The book names its subject
text: Hugo says what the whole novel is about: the march 'from evil to good, from night to day, from appetite to conscience, from nothingness to God'. Matter at the start, the soul at the end; 'the hydra at the beginning, the angel at the end'. It is a key to the light and darkness he has used since the bishop's candlesticks.

title: John Brown before Washington
text: Hugo says he venerates the 'confessors of Utopia' most in defeat, preferring martyrdom to success, 'John Brown to Washington'. John Brown, the American abolitionist, was hanged in December 1859 after his raid on Harpers Ferry. Hugo had publicly pleaded for his life, so the name was fresh when he wrote this.

title: The roll of the slain
text: 'Bossuet was killed; Feuilly was killed; Courfeyrac was killed.' After the long build-up, Hugo gives each friend half a line. The flat repetition is the epic catalogue cut down to its bare form, as in Homer's lists of the fallen. A peasant recruit and a pale student, he insists, cast a shadow as long as any Ajax.

title: Combeferre lifts a soldier
text: Combeferre, the gentle philosopher who begged Enjolras to spare the artillery sergeant, dies pierced by three bayonets 'as he lifted a wounded soldier'. He dies helping one of the enemy. Hugo gives him a glance towards heaven and nothing more.

title: Sheltered and exposed
text: Enjolras, who holds the whole defence in his head, shelters himself and is untouched. Marius fights with half his body above the breastwork, 'a phantom firing a gun', his face vanishing under blood. One man fights to win; the other came to die. Hugo puts them at the two ends of the barricade.

title: A door that does not open
text: Hemmed in, some of the defenders hammer at the door of the tall house at the back, begging to be let in. No one opens. From the third-floor window the murdered porter's head looks down on them. The chapter before argued that a city disowns a rising by shutting its doors. Here the argument becomes one door and some men beating on it.

title: The only two kisses of his life
text: Before the last fight Enjolras bends over Mabeuf and Gavroche and kisses the old man's hanging hand, as he kissed his brow the night before: 'the only two kisses of his life'. The man whose mistress is Patria gives his tenderness to an old man he hardly knew.

title: Heroism become monstrous
text: The barricade fought like a gate of Thebes, the wine-shop like a house of Saragossa. Then the last cartridges are gone, and the men on the first floor fight with bottles of aquafortis. Hugo says it resembled 'Milton and Dante rather than Homer': demons attacking, spectres resisting. He refuses to make the end glorious.

title: Orestes and Pylades
text: In Greek legend Pylades was the friend who stood by Orestes through exile and madness, ready to die in his place. Hugo's title makes Enjolras the fasting Orestes and Grantaire the drunken Pylades. The pair of the austere believer and the sceptic is given the most famous friendship of antiquity.

title: 'Do you permit it?'
text: Grantaire wakes in the silence, understands, and walks to the wall: 'Long live the Republic! I'm one of them.' Then, gently: 'Do you permit it?' Enjolras, who called him incapable of believing or dying, presses his hand with a smile. 'You will see,' Grantaire once said. He believed in nothing but Enjolras, and here he acts on it.

title: Shooting a flower
text: Enjolras, unwounded after twenty-four hours, 'fresh and rosy', compels his killers to kill him respectfully; a witness spoke of an insurgent they called Apollo, and a guardsman says he feels he is about to shoot a flower. Pierced by eight bullets, he stays upright 'as though nailed there'. Hugo makes his death almost a statue.

title: Silence wakes a drunkard
text: Grantaire has snored through fusillade, cannon and assault, so like the corpses that no one noticed him. 'Noise does not rouse a drunkard, silence does.' Hugo's small observation sets up the scene's turn: the moment the fighting stops is the moment the doubter wakes.

title: He never took his eyes off him
text: 'The hand that gripped him as he fell was Jean Valjean's.' Hugo now tells us what the barricade did not see: Valjean 'had seemed not to see Marius and had never taken his eyes off him'. He fought only by carrying the wounded. The man he wished dead the night before is the one he watched over all day.

title: Once Cosette, now Marius
text: Trapped with no way out, Valjean finds a loose grating and drops into the dark with Marius on his back. He remembers the wall of the convent garden, eight years ago, when what he carried was Cosette. 'What he carried now was not Cosette but Marius.' Hugo repeats an old escape with a different burden.

title: Below the noon
text: Above, the June sun, the assault, the tocsin. Three metres down, 'profound peace, absolute silence and night'. The noise of the taken wine-shop reaches Valjean only as a murmur. Hugo moves his hero from the most public place in Paris into the most hidden one in a single paragraph.
